title: Forgiving in traffic
hookLine: Marcus Aurelius starts his morning expecting rude people, and calls them kin
tomorrow: why did a cook who hated the kitchen call it his best place to pray?

cards: A car slides across two lanes with no signal, and you're the one slamming the brakes. A heart can be pounding before anyone's decided anything.
The emperor whose notebook opened with thank-yous, Marcus Aurelius, has another entry for exactly that kind of morning.
It begins like a man bracing for traffic: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial."

teach.b: It sounds grim. Read on, and it turns. Why are people like that?
Marcus answers: they act out of ignorance of what is good and evil. They don't see what he sees. Then he goes further.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO WRONGS ME IS KIN.
teach.b: The one who wrongs him is his kin, not by blood, but because every person shares the same reason, a portion of the divine. So he can't be harmed by them, and he can't hate them.
"For we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth."

That's the Stoic teaching, and it's specific: those who do wrong do it from not knowing the good, and every human being belongs to one shared order with you. So forgiving the driver isn't pretending they were right.
The wrong is still a wrong. It's remembering two things, fast: they don't see what you see, and they're part of the same body you are. Upper teeth don't take revenge on the lower ones.
In plain words, at a red light: they're having a day, and they're still kin.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius rehearse Meditations 2.1 in the morning, expecting difficult people and reminding themselves that those people act from not knowing and are still kin.

s: Marcus wrote that each morning he should expect arrogant, deceitful people
Meditations 2.1 opens that way, then says the one who does wrong is his kin.
Marcus calls the rude his enemies, to be beaten
he says he can't hate them: we're made for cooperation, like upper and lower teeth.
forgiving means agreeing the other person was right
the popular mix-up. for Marcus the wrong stays wrong; they act from not knowing, and they're kin.

games.q: a coworker takes credit for your idea in the morning meeting, and you're furious. what's the Marcus Aurelius move?
o: name it calmly later, remembering he acts from not knowing, and he's still kin.
feel nothing at all: a real Stoic is never bothered by anything anyone does.
get even first: the Stoics say every wrong must be answered in kind.
games.why: Marcus expects wrongdoers and still calls them kin, made to work together like teeth. the wrong can be named; the hatred isn't needed.

practice: Bring to mind one driver, or anyone, who cut in front of you lately. Breathe in and say quietly, they don't see what I see. Breathe out and say, and they're still my kin, and let them drive on.

wordCard.voice: Forgiving in traffic: the Stoic move at the wheel. They act from not knowing, and they're still kin, like upper and lower teeth.

orig.note: Greek: to himself, the old title of the notebook we call the Meditations.

carryVoice: Take this with you: they're having a day. Marcus would add, and they're still my kin. Three of fourteen.
